name: Carnivore diet

card.summary: An animal-foods-only diet promoted online for skin, leanness and jaw definition; human evidence is sparse and mainly raises nutrient and cholesterol questions.
card.note: A 2026 scoping review found nine human studies of very limited quality, with reported nutrient shortfalls and raised LDL cholesterol.

quick.overview:
The carnivore diet restricts food to animal products such as meat, eggs and dairy, excluding fruit, vegetables and grains. Its modern popularity dates from around 2018, and it appears in looksmaxxing communities as a way to get leaner, clearer skin or a better jaw and body composition.
Human evidence is thin. A 2026 scoping review located nine human studies and described the quality of evidence as very limited because of small samples, short durations and a lack of controls. Studies of appearance outcomes such as skin or facial structure were not found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say eliminating plant foods removes irritants and processed foods and increases protein and fat intake, which they link to leanness, hormone levels or skin. Reviewers describe the diet as a form of ketogenic eating with unclear long-term effects on nutrients and metabolism.
quick.risks: Reviews report potential shortfalls of vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fiber, and higher LDL and total cholesterol. Wikipedia reports that dietetic bodies, including the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia, reject the diet, and that high red meat intake is linked to higher risks of colon cancer and gout.

lead: The carnivore diet, also called the zero-carb diet, is an eating pattern in which nearly all food comes from animals: meat, fish, eggs and, for many followers, some dairy, with fruit, vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds left out. [1][2][3] In appearance-focused communities it is used as a body-composition and skin strategy: followers aim for leanness through a high-protein, satiating, low-carbohydrate pattern, and some report clearer skin or less puffiness, or pair it with training for a more muscular, defined physique. [4][5][6]

The modern movement dates to around 2018, when former orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker published a book on the diet and Jordan Peterson and his daughter Mikhaila Peterson described a strict beef, salt and water version called the lion diet; later influencers such as Paul Saladino popularised an animal-based variant that adds fruit and honey. [3][7][8] Wikipedia traces antecedents to nineteenth-century meat regimens such as James H. Salisbury's. [3]

Research on carnivore eating specifically is small. A 2026 scoping review located nine human studies and described their quality as very limited, reporting weight loss, greater satiety and possible improvements in some inflammatory or metabolic markers alongside possible nutrient shortfalls and higher LDL cholesterol; a 2021 survey of 2,029 self-selected followers described their self-reported health. [1][9] Dietetic organisations and nutrition scientists, as reported by Wikipedia, regard it as a fad diet and cite concerns about cardiovascular risk, fibre and micronutrients. [3] No published trial has examined its effects on skin or facial appearance.

chain: Cuts diet down to meat, eggs and fish
High protein and fat raise fullness and can lower calorie intake
Weight and fat loss produce a leaner, more defined face and body
Some followers also report calmer skin
angle.text: Followers use the diet as a simplified cutting and clean-eating approach: fewer food choices, high protein and strong satiety, aimed at a leaner face and physique. Some also report clearer or less inflamed skin after removing sugar and processed foods, which is a personal report rather than a trial result.

paras: Carnivore eating is described in the literature as a newly popular, sparsely studied form of ketogenic diet in which plant foods are removed so that all or nearly all nutrition comes from animal-sourced foods. [2] No standardised definition exists, which complicates research and comparison between studies. [1]

Variants differ mainly in strictness. Wikipedia lists a common pattern of beef, pork, poultry and seafood with dairy and eggs for some followers, and a stricter lion diet limited to beef, salt and water. [3] Grokipedia describes flexible 'ketovore' versions and notes that many followers eat fatty cuts to satiety, include organ meats and animal fats, and drink mainly water. [10] Wikipedia describes a 'carnivore traditionalism' strand that favours grass-fed beef and small-farm eggs and opposes industrial livestock production, and Paul Saladino's 'animal-based' diet, which keeps red meat central but adds fruit, honey and raw dairy; Wikipedia says some carnivore advocates have shifted to it because the original is hard to sustain. [3][8] Wikipedia also notes that the diet is often confused with traditional Inuit eating, which included organ meats, seafood and locally gathered plant foods. [3]

Wikipedia traces animal-only eating regimens to the nineteenth century: German writer Bernard Moncriff's 1856 book promoted an exclusively animal diet, Italian physician Arnaldo Cantani prescribed one to diabetic patients in the 1870s, and American physician James H. Salisbury advocated lean beef and hot water for several weeks in the 1880s. [3] Salisbury (1823 to 1905) described his food as the muscle pulp of beef, and the ground-beef 'Salisbury steak' takes its name from him. [11] Grokipedia also cites explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson's all-meat year under medical observation in the 1920s, a claim from an AI-generated page that should be read with that caveat. [10]

The contemporary movement grew through social media and podcasts in the late 2010s. Wikipedia reports that Shawn Baker, a former orthopaedic surgeon, promoted the diet online and wrote The Carnivore Diet in 2018, and that Jordan and Mikhaila Peterson became prominent advocates that year, with the lion diet later circulating as a viral TikTok trend. [3] Mikhaila Peterson, born in 1992, began the diet in 2018 and describes improved health, discussing it on her blog and later podcast; her Wikipedia article records that the blog drew criticism after her Joe Rogan Experience appearance. [7]

Advocates argue that human physiology evolved around meat eating, citing hominin meat consumption over millions of years and a gut anatomy they describe as suited to protein and fat. [10] They also hold that animal foods are more bioavailable sources of protein, heme iron, vitamin B12 and preformed vitamin A, and that plant defensive compounds such as lectins, oxalates and phytates can irritate the gut or bind minerals; they say removing plants simplifies digestion and cuts inflammatory triggers. [10] Ketosis, stable blood glucose and the satiating effect of protein are cited as mechanisms for fat loss. [10]

A 2024 modelling study assessed the micronutrient adequacy of four versions of the diet against national reference values, in the context of anecdotal claims of benefit for inflammatory conditions. [12] A 2020 review concluded that metabolic effects of ketogenic diets can alter nutrient needs but that hypotheses conflict, and discussed the nutritional implications of relying only on animal foods. [2]

sections.h: Use for appearance and in looksmaxxing culture
paras: Looksmaxxing members discuss the diet as a way to cut body fat, change skin or improve body composition. Looksmax.org threads include one describing how carb deprivation and a carnivore diet changed the poster's results, one weighing the diet against isotretinoin for skin, and one from a long-term follower who started as a teenager. [4][6][13] Other threads argue against it on gut, cardiovascular and cost grounds or describe raw-meat versions as 'cope'. [5][14][15] A thread ranks it alongside mewing and chewing practices, treated sceptically by its author. [16] A member describing quiet, incremental improvements to leanness, haircut and tan lists the gym and a carnivore diet among the changes. [17]

The Liver King persona, Brian Johnson, born in 1978, drew a wide online following from 2021 with a raw-meat and organ-heavy 'ancestral' lifestyle and co-owns the Heart and Soil supplement company with Paul Saladino. [18][8] In late 2022 leaked emails showed he spent heavily on steroids and other performance drugs, and he later said he took testosterone; a 2025 Netflix documentary covered the story and, per Wikipedia, he has since criticised the carnivore diet he promoted. [18] This episode is discussed in physique communities as a reminder that muscular results attributed to a diet may involve other factors.

A 2026 scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines searched four databases and included nine human studies. Individual studies reported weight reduction, increased satiety and possible improvements in inflammatory or metabolic markers; the review also identified potential shortfalls in vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre, raised LDL and total cholesterol, and one case of deteriorating health. The authors rated evidence quality as very limited because of small samples, short durations and absent control groups. [1]

A social-media survey of 2,029 adults who eat this way, published in 2021 in Current Developments in Nutrition, gathered self-reported eating habits and health status; as a self-selected descriptive survey it cannot show cause and effect. [9] A 2024 case series described ten patients using a carnivore-ketogenic diet for inflammatory bowel disease. [19] A 2025 narrative review of eight dietary strategies after acute coronary syndromes and a 2025 review of carnivore and ketogenic-like diets for paediatric obesity have also discussed the diet, the latter proposing it as an alternative approach. [20][21] A 2026 review of common diet questions includes one on whether data on the carnivore diet exist. [22]

No studies found examining the diet's effect on skin, jaw structure or facial appearance. Wikipedia's article on the better-studied ketogenic diet lists constipation, raised blood lipids and, in children, kidney stones and slowed growth among its adverse effects, and does not mention acne. [23]

The 2026 scoping review lists vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre as potential shortfalls and elevated LDL and total cholesterol as a risk. [1] Wikipedia reports concerns about raised LDL and cardiovascular disease, low fibre and constipation, colon cancer and gout associated with high red-meat intake in meta-analyses, and possible effects of high protein on kidney function. [3] A 2025 systematic review concluded that meat supports short-term hypertrophy while pathways such as mTOR and IGF-1 activation, advanced glycation end products and homocysteine may carry longevity-related costs. [24]

Advocates respond that modelled versions with organ meats and seafood can meet most nutrient reference values, that survey respondents report high satisfaction, and that nutrient needs differ on a ketogenic metabolism. [12][9][2] Paul Saladino, who called plants a poison in his 2020 book The Carnivore Code, later moved to an animal-based diet that includes fruit and honey, citing side effects he had experienced on a strict version such as poor sleep and lower testosterone, according to Wikipedia. [8]

Wikipedia reports that nutrition scientists have called the diet an extreme fad, that the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia list it among fad diets, and that neurologist Steven Novella wrote in 2023 that its cost makes it a diet for select elites. [3] Coverage the article cites includes The Independent and The Atlantic in August 2018, The Guardian on the Peterson diet in September 2018, and The New York Times in April 2024. [3] Critics also raise the environmental footprint of large-scale livestock production. [3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the carnivore diet is both promoted as a leanness and skin strategy and argued against on health, cost and cope grounds, while influencers outside the forum frame it as an ancestral or healing diet. [4][5][6][7]

claims.claim: A carnivore diet changes your game, body and skin.
claims.believers: Members describe carb deprivation and meat-only eating as changing their appearance and results, and some weigh it against isotretinoin for skin. [4][6]
claims.experts: No studies found on skin or facial appearance; the 2026 scoping review found limited evidence for weight and marker changes. [1]

claims.believers: Advocates say animal foods are highly bioavailable and that varied versions with organ meats meet reference values. [10][12]
claims.experts: Reviews report possible deficiencies of vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre; a 2020 review says evidence on plant-free adequacy is conflicting. [1][2]

claims.claim: Plant foods are harmful and removing them heals the body.
claims.believers: Followers cite lectins, oxalates and phytates and personal reports of resolved symptoms; Saladino's book calls plants poison. [10][8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that dietetic bodies reject the diet; Saladino himself later added fruit and honey. [3][8]

claims.claim: The diet harms digestion and heart health.
claims.believers: A forum poster argues that lack of fibre damages the gut microbiome and that it affects arteries. [5]
claims.experts: Reviews report raised LDL and total cholesterol in some studies, and Wikipedia lists constipation and colon cancer risk with high red-meat intake. [1][3]

claims.claim: Meat builds muscle and the leanest physiques.
claims.believers: Physique followers say high protein supports hypertrophy and satiety. [24]
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review agrees meat aids short-term hypertrophy but links it to longevity-related pathways. [24]

claims.claim: Raw-meat and organ-heavy ancestral eating gives elite physiques.
claims.believers: Liver King promoted raw organ meats as the basis of his look. [18]
claims.experts: Leaked emails showed large steroid spending and he later said he took testosterone; medical professionals called the diet potentially dangerous. [18]

claims.claim: Carnivore eating improves jaw and bone structure.
claims.believers: Forum posts credit natural, hard-chewing animal foods with better bones. [16][14]
claims.experts: No studies found on jaw or facial bone change from this diet.
